Chapter 9 · The Outbreak
of War

The Nazi–Soviet Pact, invasion of Poland and the interlocking causes of war in September 1939.

4 topic lessons + exam workshop40 topic questions25 mixed questions6 GCSE practices

All written historical-source extracts appear as full typed text; images are retained for visual evidence, with their provenance and analysis alongside.

9.1A
23 August 1939 · pp 78–79

The Nazi–Soviet Pact · why the enemies agreed

Why Hitler wanted Poland

Hitler sought Lebensraum in the east, territory that had formerly belonged to Germany and a route to unite more German-speakers. Britain and France had failed to stop earlier expansion, but they had now pledged to protect Poland.

The problem of two fronts

Invading Poland risked bringing Germany into conflict with France and Britain in the west and the USSR in the east. Hitler wanted to prevent Soviet intervention while he attacked Poland.

What the pact promised

On 23 August 1939 the German and Soviet foreign ministers, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov, signed a non-aggression treaty. A secret protocol divided spheres of influence in Eastern Europe, including Poland.

Why Stalin trusted the Western powers less

Stalin had seen the League's weaknesses in Manchuria and Abyssinia, France and Britain's reaction to the Rhineland, and the Munich settlement reached without Soviet involvement. Suspicion, diplomacy and security calculations pushed him towards a temporary deal with Hitler.

Read the sources · what the imagery means

Source A: the uneasy figures suggest an unnatural political relationship between bitter ideological opponents. Ask why the bear has a knife and what the cartoonist implies about trust.

Source B: the bride-and-groom metaphor makes the alliance look temporary, unexpected and insincere. “Honeymoon” implies that the partnership will not remain harmonious.

Provenance: these cartoons show contemporary reactions; they do not establish the private intentions of either leader.

Why did Stalin change partners?

1934–1936

Stalin joined the League, considered Franco-Soviet cooperation, then watched France fail to prevent remilitarisation of the Rhineland.

1938

The USSR was excluded from the Munich Conference. Stalin feared Western governments hoped Germany would expand eastwards.

1939

Talks with Britain and France faltered. The Soviet leadership doubted that Poland and the West would cooperate effectively with the USSR.

August 1939

The pact bought the USSR time to prepare, offered territorial gains and reduced the immediate likelihood of a German attack.

4-mark cartoon source: describe a specific visual detail, explain the message, then use contextual knowledge to explain the 1939 Nazi–Soviet agreement. Avoid saying the cartoon proves the alliance was sincere.
9.1B
The secret protocol · pp 80–81

The Nazi–Soviet Pact · motivations and significance

Stalin's calculations

Stalin hoped to regain territory in eastern Poland without immediately fighting Germany; to buy time for Soviet rearmament; and to create a buffer zone between the USSR and Germany. He did not assume Hitler had abandoned anti-Communism permanently.

Hitler's calculations

The agreement enabled Hitler to invade Poland without an immediate Soviet military response, avoid the danger of a simultaneous two-front war and pursue eastern expansion with greater confidence.

What Britain and France understood

The pact raised the danger of war. Britain and France had promised to defend Polish independence, and the pact removed a major potential deterrent to Hitler.

Why it was a turning point

On 1 September Germany invaded Poland. On 17 September the USSR invaded from the east. The pact helped both regimes act, despite their incompatible ideologies.

Evidence to evaluate: three written sources

Source C · Chamberlain’s diary, 26 March 1939
“I must confess to the most profound mistrust of Russia. I have no belief whatever in her ability to maintain an effective offensive...”

A private diary can reveal British distrust, though it is one politician’s perspective written months before the pact.

Source E · Stalin explaining the pact in 1941
“We secured peace for our country for eighteen months, which enabled us to make military preparations.”

A retrospective public justification after Germany invaded the USSR. Useful for Soviet reasoning, but consider its purpose and hindsight.

Source F analysis

Look for the figures marked “Nazi Germany” and “Soviet Russia”, both posing a threat to the figure labelled “Poland”. The fairy-tale imagery suggests Poland is vulnerable to two predatory powers. The cartoon is critical of the agreement; it is an American political interpretation rather than a secret diplomatic record.

12-mark usefulness answer: use content + contextual knowledge + provenance + limitation for each source. Source E can show Stalin's stated reason for the pact; Source F can show contemporary fears about what it meant for Poland. Finish with a balanced judgement.
9.2
1–3 September 1939 · pp 82–83

The invasion of Poland and declaration of war

Three days that changed Europe

1 September 1939

Germany invades

German troops attacked Poland. The invasion followed the Nazi–Soviet Pact and came despite Britain and France's guarantee to Poland.

3 September · morning

British ultimatum

Britain demanded German withdrawal from Poland. No satisfactory response arrived by the deadline.

3 September · 11 am

War declared

Britain declared war on Germany. France also declared war later that day. A European war had begun.

How Germany attacked

Germany used a large-scale invasion with ground forces and air support. The attack on the Polish garrison at Westerplatte near Danzig began early on 1 September; Warsaw and other cities were bombed. Polish forces were overwhelmed over the following weeks.

What happened to Poland?

The USSR invaded eastern Poland on 17 September, following the secret arrangements with Germany. Poland was defeated and occupied by two dictatorships. Britain's and France's declarations did not immediately save the country.

Source evaluation

The newspaper headline documents that the invasion became international news. The Warsaw photo supplies evidence of destruction but cannot by itself explain why Hitler decided to invade. Pair visual evidence with the date, the Polish guarantee and the pact.

Important distinction: Germany invaded on 1 September; Britain and France declared war on 3 September; Soviet troops invaded Poland on 17 September.

8-mark account: explain a chain, not just a list: the pact removed fear of Soviet intervention → Germany attacked Poland → the British ultimatum expired → Britain and France declared war.
9.3
Synthesis · pp 84–85

Why did the Second World War break out?

Historians debate the relative weight of six connected causes. The most effective answers distinguish long-term causes, enabling conditions and the immediate trigger.

1 · Hitler's foreign policy

Overturn Versailles, create a Greater Germany, acquire Lebensraum and defeat Communism. Conquest threatened the European order.

2 · Treaty of Versailles

Territorial losses and resentment furnished Nazi propaganda. The treaty also helped create new states with vulnerable borders and German minorities.

3 · Failure of the League

Manchuria and Abyssinia demonstrated the limits of collective security; the League lacked an army and great-power unity.

4 · Great Depression

Economic collapse intensified political extremism and made states less willing to bear costs of sanctions or military intervention.

5 · Appeasement

Concessions and reluctance to confront Hitler, particularly over the Rhineland and Sudetenland, shaped his confidence. Defenders argue peace and rearmament time mattered.

6 · Nazi–Soviet Pact

The August 1939 agreement removed the immediate risk of Soviet intervention against a German invasion of Poland. Britain and France then honoured their guarantee.

Historical interpretations

Traditional interpretation: Hitler's expansionist aims and deliberate aggression were central.

A. J. P. Taylor (1961): challenged the view that war was inevitable because of a uniquely predetermined Nazi foreign-policy master plan; he stressed diplomatic choices and Hitler's opportunism. This is an interpretation for evaluation, not an established fact.

Your task: judge which factor mattered most and show how at least two other factors made it more dangerous.

Grade 9 causal-link builder

Choose a combination, then explain how one factor enabled another:

Depression → League: economic distress made governments more reluctant to enforce expensive sanctions. This weakened collective security and emboldened aggressors.
16 + 4 SPaG judgement: discuss the named factor first, then at least two alternative factors using precise evidence. Weigh how directly each caused war in 1939. Finish with a clear answer to “How far do you agree?”
9.EXAM
How to write an account · pp 86–87

Exam technique workshop · 8-mark account

Step 1 · Filter events

The question asks: “Write an account of how Hitler's actions in 1938–1939 led to the outbreak of the Second World War.” Do not spend paragraphs on the Saar (1935) or Rhineland (1936). Refer to earlier developments briefly only if necessary for context.

Step 2 · Put events in order

March 1938 Anschluss → September Munich Agreement → March 1939 rest of Czechoslovakia → August Nazi–Soviet Pact → 1 September Poland → 3 September declaration of war.

Step 3 · Explain links

After each event, explain what changed and why it made the next development possible or more likely. Use therefore, as a result, this encouraged, this removed the obstacle.

Step 4 · Stay independent

Write your answer before revealing marking notes in the GCSE Practice tab. Strong answers explain a sequence of linked causes and consequences, not simply list six dates.

Self-check: Have I used accurate chronology? Have I explained the link after each event? Have I included the immediate trigger in Poland and why Britain/France declared war?

9.1A · Source message

Source B shows an unexpected alliance between Hitler and Stalin. How do you know the cartoonist presents the Nazi–Soviet Pact as unlikely to last? Use visual details and your contextual knowledge.

4 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Describe the bride and groom, the caption, and why Nazi and Soviet ideologies clashed.

The couple represent Nazi Germany and USSR; marriage metaphor; honeymoon implies the unlikely relationship may be temporary; ideologies hostile.
9.1B · Source usefulness

How useful are Source E (Stalin’s 1941 explanation) and Source F (Herblock’s 1939 fairy-tale cartoon) to a historian studying why the USSR signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact? Use both sources and contextual knowledge.

12 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Evaluate content and provenance for each source. Note the 1941 hindsight and the American cartoonist’s perspective.

E: security/time to prepare but retrospective public justification; F: contemporary perception of danger to Poland, less direct evidence of Stalin’s actual motives; conclude with balanced judgement.
9.2 · Write an account

Write an account of how Germany’s invasion of Poland led to the outbreak of war in September 1939.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Chronological order: pact, invasion on 1 September, ultimatum, declaration on 3 September. Link cause and consequence.

Hitler less concerned about USSR; attack on Poland; Polish guarantee; ultimatum to withdraw; UK declared war on 3 September; France followed.
9.3 · Judgement

“The Nazi–Soviet Pact was the main reason for the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939.” How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

16 marks + 4 SPaG
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Weigh the pact against Hitler’s aims, appeasement and the failure of the League; distinguish trigger from background causes.

Pact enabled Poland invasion; Hitler’s aggressive policy as underlying factor; appeasement/League failings as enabling conditions; conclude with prioritised and balanced judgement.
9.EXAM · Account workshop

Write an account of how Hitler’s actions in 1938–1939 led to the outbreak of the Second World War.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Plan six chronological steps from Anschluss to the invasion of Poland, explaining the link after each.

Anschluss March 1938; Munich September 1938; March 1939 invasion of rest of Czechoslovakia; Nazi–Soviet Pact August; Poland September; declaration of war.
9.3 · Interpretation challenge

Some historians argue Hitler was chiefly responsible for war; A. J. P. Taylor challenged the idea that his foreign policy made war inevitable. Explain two ways this debate changes how historians assess the causes of war.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Explain different weightings of intentions versus diplomacy, then support each with accurate historical examples.

Deliberate expansionist aims and aggression versus opportunism/international failures; distinguish scholarly interpretations from proof; examples Rhineland, Munich, Pact, Poland.
